All code should have single, well-defined responsibilities. **Single Responsibility Principle:** Each class or module should have a single, well-defined responsibility. **Open/Closed Principle:** The system should be extensible without modification; add features through new classes or modules. **Liskov Substitution Principle:** Subclasses should be substitutable for base classes without altering correctness. **Interface Segregation Principle:** Clients should not depend on unused implementation details. **Dependency Inversion Principle:** High-level modules should depend on abstractions, not low-level modules.

Avoid duplicating logic and functionality across multiple files.
Refactor repetitive code blocks into reusable components; document reusable components clearly. Strive for simplicity and readability; minimize complexity. Avoid over-engineering solutions.
Only implement functionality that is currently required.
Don't introduce features or code that is not explicitly needed.
Focus on working code, not anticipating future requirements.

Use consistent formatting and a style guide; indentation should be consistent (2 spaces). Use meaningful names and clear file names. Each file should be cohesive; separate concerns into modules. Include a README with an overview and instructions. Code length should be limited to 180 lines; each function or class should ideally be under 60 lines. Avoid unnecessary statements or blank lines. Use inline comments judiciously for complex logic; add docstrings to all functions, classes, and modules.
